newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Wary central bank punctures soaring S.African rand.
newsitem.headline: Wary central bank punctures soaring S.African rand.

text.p: South Africa's recovering rand faltered on Tuesday after Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals welcomed the currency's new year strength but warned it may have been somewhat overdone.
"I think there is a little bit of an over-adjustment," Stals told Reuters.

His comment stopped the rand's rally dead in its tracks, carving seven cents out of the rand as it weakened from a new 6 1/2 month high of 4.3790 bid against the dollar to 4.4530 before recovering to around 4.44 by the local close.
An excessive appreciation in the rand could cause problems for the economy, just as last year's excessive fall had done, Stals said.

"Just as a depreciation creates problems, so can appreciation also create problems. So we would not like to see the appreciation going on forever. But at this stage from an anti-inflationary point of view we welcome the development."

Analysts said the influential central bank governor appeared to have made a calculated bid to defuse some of the market's over-enthusiasm which has seen the rand surge some seven percent against the dollar and 14 percent against the mark this year.

"I think his concerns are that things may be moving too far, too quickly and that from a trade perspective it isn't in our interest that the rand should strengthen appreciably further from here," said Carole Mason, group economist at Investec.

The rand fell nearly 30 percent against the dollar in 1996 and 23 percent on a trade-weighted basis against a basket of currencies on fears worries about South Africa's political stability and the pace of economic reforms.

Improving trade figures have helped the rand recover this year. Economists expect a sharp improvement in South Africa's balance of trade in 1997, helping build foreign currency reserves from current precariously low levels. But this could be undermined if the rand rallies too fast, hurting exports.

Stals told a briefing in parliament that the balance of payments position would improve sharply in 1997, which in turn would help government in its decision on removing remaining foreign exchange restrictions.

But he reiterated that the Bank would advise the government to move cautiously, avoiding any one-off or "big bang" abolition of controls which prevent residents from exporting anything but very small amounts of currency.
"The Bank must...move with caution and discretion in the advice it gives to government for the gradual removal of the remaining exchange controls," he said.

He noted that steps already taken to liberalise exchange controls had resulted in about 30 billion rand ($6.75 billion) going abroad in assets swaps or direct investments over the last two and a half years.

President Nelson Mandela said last week the government remained committed to the phased removal of all controls and told state television on Monday that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel would deal fully with the issue in due course.
There has been widespread speculation the authorities will exploit the current strength of the rand to announce the next steps in easing controls around the time of the March 12 budget.
Stals threw cold water on market speculation of an early cut in interest rates, warning of the persistent risk of a further rise in inlfation.
"An over-accomodative monetary policy at this stage would be very dangerous," he said. "Maybe interest rates can decline, but later in the year with the emphasis on later."
